summary:
New Caledonia is a French collectivity. It stands under the French national framework: France retains responsibility for penal law, civil-status documents, the justice system and the prison service, while the collectivity legislates locally on many domestic matters. The protections a trans visitor would rely on are French national provisions, applying here because French law governs.

Provisions extending to New Caledonia include the Penal Code ground of discrimination on gender identity, in that wording since 18 November 2016 and previously drafted as sexual identity from July 2012; the Labour Code bar on exclusion from recruitment, sanction, dismissal or other discriminatory measures on that ground; transphobic motive as an aggravating factor for crimes punishable by imprisonment since 2017; the conversion-therapy ban published 1 February 2022; placement of detainees by legal gender marker rather than anatomy under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code; and the marriage law signed 18 May 2013, under which a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can marry in New Caledonia.

France's detention-places watchdog CGLPL reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty, a finding that by its terms covers establishments here. Its referrals since 2010 covered some forty transgender persons, and its on-site inspections at four establishments in France interviewed eight trans women and one trans man; no inspection of a New Caledonian establishment is documented.

The inventory records no New Caledonia-specific law, enforcement action, incident, institution or statistic bearing on trans visitors, and no local ordinance narrowing the national protections. No region-specific signal was identified beyond the extension of the French framework, and the national assessment for France applies.
tangentialFactors:
French police recorded around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019, up 36 per cent from around 1,380 in 2018. These are France-wide figures with no New Caledonia breakdown, so they cannot be read as a local rate; the inventory contains no comparable New Caledonian count for any year.

France declassified gender dysphoria as a diagnosis by decree in 2010 and has permitted gender-affirming surgery in country since 1979, with transsexualism carried under a long-term-illness scheme funded by the national social-security system. New Caledonia administers its own health arrangements, and no source in the inventory states whether those national funding pathways operate here.

A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location in French gender care, and the national medical academy characterised rising demand as an epidemic-like phenomenon and a primarily social problem while advising caution without changing practice. Both are France-wide findings; no New Caledonia-specific care-access evidence is sourced.
localsOnly:
Residents of New Caledonia change legal gender through the French court process established by the law signed 18 November 2016 following the Constitutional Council ruling of 17 November 2016, in force 1 January 2017, which requires no surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificate or medical diagnosis but still requires an application to a court. A first-name change can be made at a registry office.

Residents are covered by Penal Code article 225-1 on gender identity, by the Labour Code prohibition on discriminatory measures in recruitment, sanction and dismissal, and by the aggravating-factor rule for crimes motivated by transphobia that has applied since 2017. No local divergent procedure or narrower ordinance is documented.

Residents held in custody are placed according to their legal gender marker under Article D248, which in practice places trans women in all-male facilities where they face threats of assault from other detainees, according to a French news feature of 12 January 2018. No New Caledonia-specific account of conditions in local establishments is sourced.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the French national health-funding arrangements for gender-affirming care, including the long-term-illness scheme covering transsexualism, extend to New Caledonia's separate health administration is unresolved; no source in the inventory addresses it.

Whether Article D248 placement practice is applied in New Caledonian establishments is asserted only as an extension of French law. No inspection, prosecution, complaint or incident inside New Caledonia is documented, and the CGLPL inspections cited were conducted at establishments in France.

A bill to ban medical transition under age 18 passed the French Senate in May 2024, had no update after 23 July 2024, is opposed by the Macron government and is regarded as unlikely to clear the National Assembly. Whether it would extend to New Caledonia if enacted, and whether it will be enacted, are unresolved.

The most recent France-wide violence figures in the inventory close in 2019 and the most recent detention-watchdog finding is dated 25 May 2021. No later New Caledonia-specific instance of any harm in this assessment is documented, and an undocumented present should not be read as a safe one.
